claims.text: The proposed framework would be trained on high-throughput DFT data for HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The framework can predict phonon and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions separately.
The framework will have 20–30% lower prediction error than previous single-channel or Debye-based models.
The claimed predictive improvement applies from 100 K to 1200 K.
The initial sample contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr sample is a homogeneous, single-phase BCC solid solution with minimal secondary phases.
The proposed approach combines ab initio simulations with explicit phonon–electron scattering models and representations of atomic disorder and oxygen impurities.
Phonon and electronic heat-transport channels can be treated separately rather than inferred only as a total conductivity.
Atomic disorder produces enhanced thermal-carrier scattering in the homogeneous BCC phase.

Treating chemical complexity, impurity scattering, and phonon and electron transport together will improve conductivity predictions over conventional Debye-like or purely first-principles approximations.
The ML model will resolve sub-lattice variations and temperature-dependent scattering more accurately than conventional approaches.
Prior approaches yield total thermal conductivities of 10–17 W/(m·K) over approximately 300–1200 K.
Existing DFT-based or analytical models do not fully capture both lattice and electronic pathways or oxygen-impurity effects.
Existing models have lower predictive accuracy than the proposed framework.
The model is applicable only to single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen between 100 K and 1200 K.
Model accuracy depends on representative training data, consistent experimental calibration, and correct treatment of defect distributions.
Prediction uncertainty will increase for more complex microstructures or oxygen concentrations above the proposed range.
Electrical resistivity and Seebeck measurements can be used to determine the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity.
Inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering can determine the phonon contribution to thermal conductivity.
A measured total or partial conductivity differing from the prediction by more than approximately 30% would falsify the hypothesis.
